core: Working definition of energy balance: the relationship between energy taken in through food and drinks and energy used by the body (attributed to FDA guidance and the OpenStax-derived text)
Three states: neutral (weight generally maintained), positive (surplus stored, weight generally rises over time), negative (stores drawn on, weight generally falls over time)
What uses energy: basal needs (largest share), digestion, physical activity (most variable)
Honest note: calories-in-vs-out is a simplification; the body is not a simple ledger (sleep, medicines, health conditions, genes, individual variation)
Weight and balance: general factual relationship, no diet advice
Measuring it: food records and label reading for intake; activity trackers and apps for movement; estimates, not precision
Honest framing: balance is a long-run average across weeks and months, not a daily score
supporting: Energy intake and expenditure are each influenced by factors partly outside conscious control
Surplus energy may be stored or used for growth; shortfalls draw on the body's stores
Original arithmetic worked example of a week's surplus and shortfall
outOfScope: What a calorie is, per-gram energy values (4-4-9-7), and label-calorie mechanics -> nutrition:foundations:energy-and-calories (own topic; referenced only)
Metabolic pathways, metabolic rate determinants, and thermic-effect depth -> nutrition:foundations:metabolism (own topic)
Eating-behavior psychology (appetite control, emotions, disordered eating) -> psychology subject (own topic)
Reading every part of the Nutrition Facts label -> nutrition:foundations:nutrition-labels (own topic)
Diet advice, weight-loss programs, or weight-management recommendations -> not part of this lesson

claims.claim: Energy balance is the relationship between the energy a person takes in through food and drinks and the energy the body uses; the body is in balance when energy intake roughly equals energy expended.

There are three states of energy balance: neutral (intake roughly matches use, weight generally maintained), positive (intake exceeds use, the surplus is stored, weight generally rises over time), and negative (intake falls short, the body draws on its stores, weight generally falls over time).

The body uses energy in three broad ways: basal needs (basic life-support processes at rest, usually the largest share, on the order of half to two-thirds of daily energy), digestion (processing food), and physical activity (movement, the part that varies most).

'Calories in versus calories out' is a simplification: the body is not a simple ledger, because sleep, medicines, health conditions, genes, and individual variation all affect how much a person eats and how the body uses energy, and some of those factors are outside a person's control.

Stated factually, weight tends to be maintained when balance is neutral, tends to rise with a sustained positive balance, and tends to fall with a sustained negative balance; changes show up over time, not as a daily score.

The general tools for estimating energy balance are food records (writing down what and how much you eat, aided by label reading) for the intake side and activity trackers or phone apps for the movement side; such tools give estimates, not laboratory-precision measurements.
Energy balance is best read as a long-run average: what matters is the pattern of intake and use across weeks and months, single days wobble around the trend, and occasional setbacks are normal.

Worked example (original, arithmetic verified): Dana's daily needs are about 2,200 calories; on five days at 2,500 she takes in 1,500 surplus calories (5 x 300), on two days at 2,000 she falls 400 short (2 x 200), leaving about 1,100 surplus for the week; a week running 200 calories short each day would draw about 1,400 calories from stores.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Some popular materials present 'calories in versus calories out' as exact, daily arithmetic that fully explains weight change.
positions: The in-out relationship is often stated as a simple equation with weight change as its direct result.

Authoritative sources (NIDDK, OpenStax-derived text) describe the relationship as a general tendency over time, with sleep, medicines, health conditions, genes, and individual variation influencing both sides.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the general relationship factually and explicitly notes the simplification, so readers get the honest version without the false precision.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained only generic boilerplate ('Energy Balance is a foundational concept in Nutrition') and no substantive claims; nothing in it was retained.

sourceRecords.title: OpenStax Nutrition (Nutrition for Nurses) 2e, Section 1.1: What Is Nutrition?
sourceRecords.notes: Read via Wayback Machine capture of 2024-04-12 (openstax.org blocks direct fetching). States 'Human bodies need calories to function, digest food, grow, and move,' that calorie needs vary by age, sex, and activity level, and that counting calories is one way to gauge whether intake meets needs. Supports the three broad uses of food energy (function, digest, move) and the measuring-it section.

sourceRecords.title: Weight Control (Health Topic)
sourceRecords.notes: Verified 2026-08-22. States 'You gain weight when you take in more calories (through food and drinks) than you use up from physical activity and daily living,' that a healthy weight involves 'a balance of food and activity,' and that sleep, emotions, medicines, and health conditions can all affect weight. Supports the three states, the weight relationship, and the honest note that balance is not purely arithmetic.

sourceRecords.title: Metabolism (Medical Encyclopedia)
sourceRecords.notes: Verified 2026-08-22 (review date 7/15/2024). Defines metabolism as all the physical and chemical processes in the body that convert or use energy and lists energy-using processes: breathing, circulating blood, controlling body temperature, contracting muscles, digesting food and nutrients, eliminating waste, and functioning of the brain and nerves. Supports the 'what uses energy' section. Metabolism mechanics beyond this list are owned by the metabolism topic.

sourceRecords.title: Calories on the Nutrition Facts Label
sourceRecords.notes: Verified 2026-08-22. States 'To achieve or maintain a healthy body weight, balance the number of calories you eat and drink with the number of calories your body uses' and that 2,000 calories a day is only a general guide. Provides the attributed working definition of energy balance used in the lesson. Label-reading depth is owned by the nutrition-labels topic.

sourceRecords.title: Factors Affecting Weight & Health
sourceRecords.provider: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK), NIH
sourceRecords.notes: Verified 2026-08-22 (last reviewed May 2023). States that taking in more calories than are used during physical activity and daily living means the body 'may store some of these extra calories as fat,' that 'over time, if you continue to take in more calories than you use, you will likely gain weight,' and that many factors affect weight: lifestyle habits, environment, sleep, medicines (which can alter energy balance), health problems, and family history and genes. Core support for the positive-balance state, the long-run framing, and the honest note.

sourceRecords.title: Eating & Physical Activity to Lose or Maintain Weight
sourceRecords.provider: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK), NIH
sourceRecords.notes: Verified 2026-08-22 (last reviewed May 2023). Recommends following progress 'using online trackers or smartphone apps that can help you keep track of the foods you eat, your physical activity, and your weight' and notes setbacks are normal and the aim is change 'over the long term.' Supports the measuring-it section (food records and activity trackers as general tools) and the long-run framing. No diet or program advice is reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: An Introduction to Nutrition (Zimmerman), Section 11.3: Balancing Energy Input with Energy Output
sourceRecords.notes: Verified 2026-08-22. States 'Energy balance is achieved when intake of energy is equal to energy expended'; in positive balance excess nutrient energy is stored or used for growth; in negative balance the body uses its stores; weight is maintained in balance, lost in negative balance, and gained in positive balance; total energy expenditure includes physical activity, basal metabolism, and digesting food; basal metabolism is typically 50-70% of daily energy use; and 'many other factors play a role in energy intake and energy expenditure. Some of these factors are under your control and others are not.'
